Table 2 compares JS design \mathrm{JS}_{\text{design}} for independently proposed designs, JS impl \mathrm{JS}_{\text{impl}} for final implementations, and the measured performance score S perf \mathrm{S}_{\text{perf}} . Each value aggregates the same 26 tasks for a model; implementation and performance scores are reported separately for each guidance configuration. Our key findings are: ( i ) Implementation scores align with performance and guidance gains. In both configurations, JS impl \mathrm{JS}_{\text{impl}} follows the broad model ordering of S perf \mathrm{S}_{\text{perf}} . Guidance also increases both scores for every model. Thus, despite having no runtime access, the judge captures both performance differences across models and the direction of improvement under guidance. ( ii ) Independent design scores also reflect broad performance differences. Higher JS design \mathrm{JS}_{\text{design}} is generally associated with stronger unguided performance. Appendix C.3 presents a concrete Muon case illustrating the design and implementation assessments. Summarized Answer to RQ2. Runtime-blind implementation scores align with broad performance differences and guidance gains. Independent design scores also reflect broad performance differences. This alignment is approximate and demonstrated across model aggregates. 4.3 RQ3: Effects of Design Guidance Levels Figure 3 : Expert-relative performance under cumulative guidance. Results are available for all three models on all 26 tasks under each input configuration. We evaluate four fixed input configurations in separate optimization runs: no guidance, L1 , L1 + L2 , and L1 + L2 + L3 . The guidance supplied in each run remains fixed. We select GPT-6-Astra, GPT-5.6-Sol, and Claude-Opus-4.8 for cumulative ablations because they produce correct implementations on all 26 tasks; all three also have correct submissions and valid timing on every workload under every ablation configuration. These cumulative configurations preserve dependencies among design decisions. Figure 3 compares their expert-relative performance using the same timing procedure and expert reference implementations as Table 1 . Values use Equations 1 and 2 with 𝒯 \mathcal{T} equal to all 26 tasks and expert latency in the numerator, and are multiplied by 100. Across all three models, performance increases at every step of the guidance sequence. For GPT-6-Astra, most of the total gain comes from adding L1 guidance, while GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-4.8 gain more from adding L3 than from adding L2 . This pattern highlights the value of guidance about GPU execution mechanisms even after algorithm and dataflow choices have been supplied. Together, the three models show how guidance at each level supports the translation of expert designs into efficient implementations. We also observe that guidance increases token usage, but the guided optimization trajectory reaches a higher final retained score; the token-efficiency results are reported in Appendix A.4 . Summarized Answer to RQ3. Averaged across the three models, adding L1 yields the largest incremental gain, while L2 and L3 provide additional improvements. 5 Related Work GPU kernel generation benchmarks. GPU kernel generation benchmarks vary in task and hardware coverage and in the reliability of their evaluation [ 9 ] . KernelBench [ 1 ] established the task of producing a correct GPU kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference; TritonBench [ 10 ] focuses on Triton operators, MultiKernelBench [ 11 ] spans GPUs, NPUs, and TPUs, and DataKernelBench [ 12 ] extends the domain to database queries. Evaluation methods also differ. Robust-kbench [ 13 ] and KernelBench-Verified [ 14 ] strengthen verification and hidden testing, while KernelBenchX [ 15 ] and AgentKernelArena [ 16 ] analyze correctness, hardware efficiency, and agent generalization. SOL-ExecBench [ 5 ] evaluates kernel performance against analytically derived hardware bounds [ 17 ] . FastKernels [ 3 ] emphasizes production interfaces, and RealisticTritonBench [ 18 ] uses framework pull requests and end-to-end tests. FlashInfer-Bench [ 19 ] studies serving workloads, while Atrex-Bench [ 20 ] samples operators and shapes from production inference traces. Kernel optimization by LLM agents. Agentic systems optimize kernels through iterative feedback, reusable knowledge, and hardware guidance. AutoKernel [ 21 ] and TritonForge [ 22 ] organize compilation, testing, profiling, and revision, while Astra [ 23 ] and CUDAMaster [ 24 ] add multi-agent or hardware-aware workflows. KernelSkill [ 25 ] provides reusable optimization knowledge. AccelOpt [ 26 ] and DRTriton [ 27 ] learn from prior implementations or synthetic data, while Xe-Forge [ 28 ] stages search under hardware constraints. KernelFoundry [ 29 ] and QiMeng-Kernel [ 30 ] use evolutionary search or hierarchical planning. Hari et al. [2] allocate search effort using a compact domain-specific language and Speed-of-Light guidance, and Shui et al. [6] show that expert directions can improve final implementations in a B200 contest harness. A complementary line of work develops programming systems that make computation, data movement, and scheduling choices explicit, including Halide [ 31 ] , Fireiron [ 32 ] , Triton [ 33 ] , and TileLang [ 34 ] . 6 Conclusion We propose D2K-Bench , a new benchmark that measures how effectively LLM agents translate expert design guidance into efficient GPU kernels. The benchmark pairs 26 tasks and 85 workloads with guidance on high-level algorithmic insights, dataflow design, and low-level optimization tricks. Its evaluation combines pairwise performance comparisons with assessments of independently proposed designs and generated code. Across five models on NVIDIA B200 GPUs, guidance raises correctness over 130 model–task pairs from 93.1% to 98.5%. The Performance Score is computed over all 26 tasks for each model and increases from 1.46 to 1.95. Guidance also raises the mean combined implementation score from 57 to 70. Guidance improves performance, but agents still leave assessed design properties unimplemented. References [1] A. Ouyang, S. Guo, S. Arora, A. L. Zhang, W. Hu, C. Ré, and A.
